I agree with the idea that attending a university should not be treated as an automatic decision for every young person. Many students enter college immediately after high school without knowing what they want to study, what kind of career they want, or even whether a university degree is necessary for their goals.

University can still be extremely valuable. It can provide specialized knowledge, professional opportunities, mentors, and access to experiences that are difficult to obtain elsewhere. However, the value of a degree depends greatly on the student's goals and on how intentionally that student uses the opportunity. Choosing a major only because of family pressure or social expectations can lead to frustration and wasted time.

For that reason, I believe students should be encouraged to explore their interests before making such an important commitment. Taking time away from school, working, learning independently, or changing majors should not automatically be viewed as failure. The most important thing is to make an informed decision. The Professional Proficiency on the Use of Force When It is Unknown if a Suspect Has a Weapon

Abstract This paper has to deal with discussing the life and death situations that occur all the time for police officers across the United States. These situations involve weapons and people. These people have the intention to use these weapons for evil rather than good. Now the problem is, what should law enforcement officers do in situations where there is a potential for a weapon to be involved, but they cannot prove beyond a reasonable doubt, at the time, that the suspect has a weapon. A law enforcement officer must be able to make a split-second decision on what to do. What should they do, one may ask? Some people believe that police officers should not use any force or only the force permitted for what the officer can confirm what the suspect possesses. Others believe that all suspects should be treated as if they are armed. This question can also be taken a step further. What force should a police officer use if it is seen that the suspect may be holding a weapon, but it cannot be confirmed if the weapon is real or not? These questions on what the correct amount of force to be used if it is unknown if the suspect possesses a weapon is what this paper will be discussing.

The Professional Proficiency on the Use of Force When It is Unknown if a Suspect Has a Weapon To shoot or not to shoot is the real question. Police officers must deal with those situations when dealing with suspects. Suspects are informed not to move while being placed under arrest, yet sometimes these people will move their hands to their body in what police officers assume they are reaching for a weapon. There are cases that people have been shot and killed by police officers when they were unarmed. So, what should police officers do in these situations? What is the most effective and efficient way to handle suspects if it cannot be confirmed if they have a weapon or not? Should police officers treat all suspects as if they are armed? Should they do absolutely nothing until they can identify a weapon and confirm the suspect was in possession of a weapon? There is a gap in training, some people say, that police officers need to be able to judge better how to handle situations, and not have discharging a firearm be the first response in a potentially dangerous situation. The National Institute of Justice (NIJ) and Federal Law Enforcement Training Center (FLETC) have composed a use-of-force continuum that includes five levels of force. They are, in order from the most non-lethal to lethal: the officer’s presence, verbalization, empty-hand control, less-lethal methods and lethal force (National Institute of Justice [NIJ], 2009). There are many ways to handle a suspect, but which is the safest and most effective, lethal or non-lethal, for the community and law enforcement officers that are involved in a life or death situation? Non-Lethal Force Officers decide on the use of force as to how a citizen is acting, which “shape[s] the actions [they] will take.” (Crawford & Burns, 2008) The use of non-lethal force has been taught to law enforcement officers to avoid unnecessary deaths when dealing with suspects. Police officers have plenty of options when using non-lethal force, which include: the officer’s presence, verbalization, and empty-hand control. These are the most used and most successful uses of force when dealing with a suspect, but will these be the best option when dealing with a suspect who possesses a weapon or if the suspect has the intent to hurt someone or the officer? With an officer’s presence, it really depends on what the situation that the officer was called to in terms of the hostility of the suspects and what actions they might take against the officer. A police officer can also use their voice to control a situation and make a suspect stop what they are doing. Although these are great tactics to maintain peace when the law enforcement officers are activated if a suspect possesses a weapon and intends to use it these tactics provide a lack of safety to the officer or the public. The last type of non-lethal uses of force is the use of empty-hand control, which includes soft and hard techniques.  Soft techniques consist of grabs, locks, and holds while hard techniques consist of punches and kicks in order to restrain an individual. These techniques are beneficial when a suspect is within arm’s reach of a law enforcement officer, but many times a suspect that has a firearm or weapon starts farther away and it is physically impossible to use these techniques to gain control of a situation. While non-lethal force is the best outcome for all situations, there is no evidence to suggest that non-lethal force is the safest way to protect the public or officer’s when a suspect is not known to possess a weapon. Less Lethal Force Another way for law enforcement officers to handle suspects when it is unknown if they have a weapon or not, but the suspect is being difficult is through the use of less lethal force. Less lethal force uses assisted devices in order to bring a suspect down. Batons, Tasers and chemicals are the typical ways that law enforcement officers take down suspects that are being difficult and the non-lethal uses of force have not or will not work. It has been a public opinion that law enforcement officers have not used the proper amount of less lethal force, but rather use excessive force which leads to lethal force when a suspect was thought to have possessed a weapon but instead the officer was mistaken and the object was not actually a weapon. Less lethal force is a great option and does work. Tasers, chemicals, and batons are useful tools in bringing down a suspect, but if that suspect has a weapon it is illogical to use certain tools. A baton is only useful for up close encounters and if the suspect has a weapon the officer is put at risk for injury if attempting to stop the suspect. Chemicals are useful in getting the suspect to stop due to pain, but just at batons require a close-up encounter. Tasers are also very effective, unless the suspect is under the influence of a substance or happens to have more body fat, both of these factors can make it illogical to use tasers at certain instances. With the use of less lethal force, it is more practical to use it, but in life or death situations will it effectively protect everyone involved? Lethal Force Law enforcement officers utilize lethal force when there is a life or death situation where the officer themselves or public safety is at risk. They are allowed “to use nearly all types of force against nearly all types of resistance…” (Terrill & Paoline, 2012), which includes lethal force if a major threat of a weapon is involved. While this is the worst-case scenario option, it is utilized to protect people in the officer’s mind. Every year “there is an annual average of 360 cases of police use of deadly force in the United States…” (Donner, Maskaly, Piquero & Jennings, 2017). All officers that use their weapons in the line of duty use them due to the fact that they believe there is a risk to personal safety of themselves or the public. There have been many cases where a suspect has been shot and killed even when it was found out that the suspect had no weapon, but due to actions of the suspect the law enforcement officers had to use lethal force in order to protect themselves and the public. Lethal force is a terrible thing to use, but if used properly and in good faith should it be allowed to be used without scrutiny? Conclusion The use of force is greatly challenged, but officers are trained to “their agency’s less lethal use of force policy” (Paoline & Terrill, 2011) in order to handle suspects in all aspects. If an officer is threatened with the potential use of a weapon, the officer has the same right as any fellow American would have in protecting themselves to discharge their firearm in protecting themselves and the public. Officers should be able to use the amount of force they deem necessary for a situation they deem to be dangerous with the immediate threat of a weapon being used.

Decision-Making and Use of Force Under Weapon Uncertainty

Police officers sometimes have only seconds to decide how to respond when a person may be armed. These situations are difficult because waiting too long can expose officers or bystanders to danger, while reacting too aggressively can injure or kill a person who did not actually present a deadly threat. The central issue is therefore not whether officers should always assume a weapon is present or always wait for absolute confirmation. A more appropriate approach is to use proportional force based on observable behavior, the immediacy of the threat, distance, available cover, and the officer’s ability to slow the situation down.

Use-of-force policies generally describe a range of options. Officer presence and verbal commands are the least intrusive. When circumstances allow, clear instructions and communication can resolve encounters without physical force. Empty-hand control can be used when a person resists and the officer can safely approach. These methods reduce the likelihood of serious injury, but they may be inappropriate if a person’s actions create an immediate threat that cannot be controlled at close range.

Less-lethal tools, such as conducted-energy devices or impact tools, can provide additional options between hands-on control and deadly force. Their usefulness depends on the circumstances. Distance, clothing, movement, the presence of other people, and the person’s physical condition can all affect whether a less-lethal tool is likely to work. Officers therefore need training that emphasizes when these tools are appropriate and when relying on them could increase danger.

Deadly force carries the greatest consequences and should be tied to an objectively reasonable belief that there is an imminent threat of death or serious bodily harm, consistent with applicable law and departmental policy. Uncertainty alone should not automatically justify lethal force. Instead, officers should evaluate specific behavior, such as visible access to a weapon, threatening movements, verbal statements, proximity, and the ability to retreat or create distance.

Training is especially important because real encounters do not unfold as simple textbook scenarios. Scenario-based exercises can expose officers to ambiguous situations in which a person reaches suddenly, ignores commands, holds an unidentified object, or behaves unpredictably. Training can also emphasize tactics that create time and distance, such as using cover, waiting for backup when feasible, and maintaining communication. These options can reduce the pressure to make an immediate irreversible decision.

The safest policy is not one that treats every person as armed or one that prevents officers from responding until a weapon is clearly visible. Both extremes ignore the complexity of real encounters. Effective use-of-force decision-making requires proportionality, evidence-based training, careful assessment of observable threats, and accountability after force is used. The goal should be to protect officers, suspects, and the public while using no more force than the situation reasonably requires.

Introduction

Vital capacity is the maximum amount of air that can be expelled from the lungs after a person takes the deepest possible breath. Because this measurement reflects the ability of the respiratory system to move air, it is commonly used in clinical and research settings. Vital capacity is measured through spirometry, a method in which a person breathes into a device that records lung volumes. Several biological and lifestyle variables may influence vital capacity. Height is frequently associated with lung volume because taller individuals generally have larger thoracic dimensions. Chest circumference may also relate to the amount of space available for lung expansion. Physical activity and athletic training can affect respiratory conditioning, while resting heart rate can provide a general indication of cardiovascular fitness. Body position may also influence measurements because the mechanics of breathing change when a person is standing, sitting, or lying down.

Although spirometry is often discussed in relation to older adults or patients with respiratory disease, studying young adults is useful because it provides information about variation in a generally healthy population. University laboratory students represent a convenient group in which differences in stature, activity level, and other characteristics can be compared under similar testing conditions.

The purpose of this study was to investigate vital capacity in university students and determine whether selected physical or lifestyle variables were associated with the measured values. text:
Why a First-Year Success Course Should Be Required

College students are expected to learn far more than the content of their major. Employers also value skills such as goal setting, time management, communication, flexibility, stress management, and professional preparation. Universities often offer workshops that teach these skills, but optional programs do not reach every student. A required first-year success course can provide all incoming students with a structured introduction to the habits they will need both in college and in the workplace.

Goal setting is one of the most important skills such a course can teach. Many students arrive on campus with general ambitions but no clear method for turning those ambitions into manageable steps. Learning to distinguish between short-term and long-term goals, monitor progress, and adjust plans can make academic work feel more controllable. Goal setting also encourages students to take responsibility for their choices rather than waiting until problems become urgent.

Time management is equally important. College schedules are less structured than high-school schedules, and students must balance classes, assignments, employment, family obligations, and social activities. Without planning, deadlines can quickly overlap. A first-year course can introduce practical techniques such as weekly scheduling, prioritization, breaking large projects into smaller tasks, and estimating how long work will take. These habits are useful in nearly every profession as well.

Stress management should also be included. Students often encounter academic pressure at the same time that they are adjusting to new social and financial responsibilities. A course cannot eliminate stress, but it can teach students how to recognize unhealthy patterns, use campus resources, and develop routines that support sleep, exercise, and realistic planning. Knowing when and where to seek help can prevent a manageable problem from becoming a crisis.

Professional preparation is another reason to require the course. Students frequently wait until graduation to think seriously about résumés, interviews, networking, and transferable skills. Introducing these topics in the first year gives students time to build experiences rather than trying to create a professional profile at the last minute. Career preparation also helps students understand how classroom skills connect to future employment.

Some students may believe they already know how to manage time or set goals. However, a required course creates a common foundation and ensures that access to these resources does not depend on whether a student happens to discover an optional workshop. The course can also be designed around practice rather than simple lectures, allowing students to apply strategies to their real schedules and goals.

A university education should prepare students to succeed academically and to continue learning after graduation. A required first-year success course supports both purposes. By teaching goal setting, time management, stress management, adaptability, and professional preparation, the university can help students develop habits that remain valuable long after a single semester ends.

text:
Improving Video-Conferencing Etiquette in Business

Video conferencing has become a routine part of professional communication. Businesses use it to interview applicants, meet with clients, coordinate international teams, and maintain relationships across distance. Although the technology makes meetings easier to schedule, successful video communication requires more than turning on a camera. Organizations should train employees in video-conferencing etiquette because nonverbal behavior, cultural and language differences, and technical quality all influence how professional messages are received.

Nonverbal communication is especially important on video. Eye contact, posture, facial expression, and visible attention all affect whether a speaker appears interested and trustworthy. In a physical meeting, people naturally notice when someone is distracted. The same is true online. Looking repeatedly at another monitor, typing while someone is speaking, or keeping the camera at an awkward angle can communicate disinterest even when that is not the employee’s intention. Training can help workers understand how camera placement, posture, facial expressions, and speaking pace influence professional impressions.

Verbal communication also changes in a virtual setting. Delays and audio problems can make interruptions more common, so employees need to pause, speak clearly, and avoid talking over others. Presenters should use an organized speaking style and should know how to explain information without relying on physical materials that remote participants cannot see. Practicing these habits can make employees more confident and reduce misunderstandings.

International video meetings create additional challenges. Different cultures may interpret eye contact, silence, directness, gestures, and turn-taking differently. Language barriers can also make fast conversation difficult. Businesses that work internationally should prepare employees for these differences and, when necessary, provide interpreters or translated materials. Cultural preparation demonstrates respect and can help prevent a communication mistake from being interpreted as a professional or personal insult.

Technology is the final part of effective video conferencing. Poor microphones, unstable internet connections, low-quality cameras, and unfamiliar software can distract from the content of a meeting. Organizations should invest in reliable equipment and teach employees how to test audio, share screens, manage presentation tools, and respond when the connection fails. A simple technical rehearsal can prevent valuable meeting time from being wasted.

Video conferencing can approximate many advantages of face-to-face communication, but only when participants know how to use the medium effectively. Businesses should therefore treat virtual communication as a professional skill. Training employees in verbal and nonverbal etiquette, cultural awareness, and technical preparation can improve productivity, reduce misunderstandings, and strengthen relationships with clients and colleagues.

A Rhetorical Analysis of Maya Angelou’s Letter to My Daughter

Maya Angelou’s Letter to My Daughter uses personal experience as a source of instruction. Rather than presenting advice as a list of abstract rules, Angelou builds her message through memories, reflection, and carefully chosen rhetorical strategies. In the excerpt, ethos, pathos, symbolism, imagery, diction, and tone work together to encourage readers—especially women—to approach difficulty with courage and to recognize that painful experiences can become sources of wisdom.

Angelou establishes ethos primarily through autobiography. She does not ask readers to trust her simply because she is a famous writer. Instead, she describes moments from her own life that reveal vulnerability, uncertainty, and growth. By writing honestly about family, adolescence, motherhood, and mistakes, she presents herself as someone whose advice comes from experience. Her public reputation strengthens that credibility, but the more important source of ethos is the openness of the narrative itself. Readers see how she reached her conclusions rather than being told to accept them.

Pathos is equally important. Angelou repeatedly connects larger lessons to emotionally specific moments. Memories involving her mother, her grandmother, insecurity, and the birth of her son create situations that readers can understand even if their own lives are different. These scenes invite the audience to feel affection, fear, uncertainty, and hope alongside the narrator. Because the advice grows out of emotion, it feels less like a lecture and more like a conversation between generations.

Symbolism allows Angelou to give ordinary events broader meaning. Home, for example, can represent more than a physical location. It can represent safety, identity, or the emotional space in which a person feels accepted. Likewise, family members can symbolize values that Angelou carries forward. Her descriptions of important people in her life help readers understand how dignity, charity, and resilience were learned through relationships.

Imagery strengthens those symbolic ideas by making memories concrete. Instead of discussing courage only as a concept, Angelou places the reader inside scenes where courage is required. The sensory and emotional details make the past vivid, which gives her later reflections more authority. The lessons feel earned because the reader has seen the experiences from which they developed.

Angelou’s diction and tone also shape the audience’s response. Her language can be direct, intimate, humorous, and serious within the same passage. That flexibility prevents the text from becoming overly sentimental. The tone suggests that hardship is real, but it does not have to define the future. She acknowledges pain while continuing to emphasize growth.

Taken together, these rhetorical strategies support Angelou’s central purpose. She encourages readers to treat their experiences as sources of knowledge rather than as permanent limitations. Ethos makes her trustworthy, pathos makes her message emotionally accessible, symbolism and imagery deepen the meaning of her memories, and diction and tone create a voice that is both authoritative and compassionate. As a result, Letter to My Daughter functions not only as autobiography but also as a form of guidance for readers learning how to interpret their own lives.

As we became older, the boundaries slowly expanded, but we still knew that disappearing without telling anyone would cause panic and punishment.

Looking back, these unwritten rules taught me more than how to avoid trouble. They taught me how a neighborhood functions. Respecting property, keeping track of time, and letting people know where you are are simple habits, but they are also ways of showing responsibility. The rules sometimes felt restrictive when I was a child, yet they helped me understand the people and expectations of the community where I grew up.

Privacy and Social Media

Social networking platforms make it easy to connect with other people, but the convenience of these services creates important privacy concerns. Users often provide personal details such as their location, interests, relationships, purchases, and browsing habits without fully understanding how those details may be collected and used. The result is that a service that feels personal can also function as a large source of behavioral data.

One common use of this information is targeted advertising. Social media companies can learn what users click on, what pages they follow, and what subjects they search for. Advertisers can then select audiences based on these characteristics. This can make advertisements more relevant, but it also means that online behavior is continuously analyzed. Many people become aware of this only when an advertisement appears shortly after they search for a product or discuss a topic online.

Another concern is data aggregation. Information from different sources can be combined to create detailed profiles of individuals. A single post may seem harmless, but when it is connected with location history, shopping behavior, search activity, and public records, it can reveal much more than the user intended. These profiles may influence marketing decisions and, in some contexts, can affect how organizations evaluate people.

Online profiling also creates the possibility of stereotyping. Algorithms may place users into categories based on patterns that do not accurately describe them. A search made for a friend, a temporary interest, or a single purchase can be interpreted as evidence of a broader characteristic. If such assumptions are used in important decisions, inaccurate data can have real consequences.

For these reasons, users should understand that privacy settings alone do not eliminate data collection. Companies should communicate clearly about what information is gathered, how long it is stored, and who can access it. Users should also be cautious about what they publish and should review privacy policies rather than treating them as meaningless agreements. Social media can be useful and entertaining, but participation should not require people to give up control over their personal information without understanding the tradeoff.

In Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie’s Purple Hibiscus, Aunty Ifeoma’s flat in Nsukka symbolizes freedom and escape for Jaja and Kambili. Their time there introduces them to a family environment that is very different from the strict and controlled life they experience under their father. Through the contrast between the two homes, Adichie shows how freedom allows the siblings to begin developing their own identities.

At home, Jaja and Kambili live according to detailed schedules and are expected to obey their father without question. Their behavior, study time, prayer, and daily routines are carefully controlled. Because punishment is always possible, they learn to remain quiet and avoid expressing disagreement.

Aunty Ifeoma’s home is different. Her children speak openly, ask questions, laugh, argue, and participate in family conversations. Jaja and Kambili are surprised by this atmosphere because they are not used to such freedom. They begin to experience ordinary activities, social interaction, and religious practices in ways that feel less restrictive.

The flat also becomes a place where Kambili grows emotionally. Her relationships with Aunty Ifeoma, her cousins, and Father Amadi help her become more confident and more aware of life outside her father’s authority. Jaja also becomes more independent and willing to question rules.

When they return home, however, the contrast becomes painful. Their father reacts harshly to behavior he considers disobedient or sinful. These punishments reveal how dangerous independence can be within his household.

Aunty Ifeoma’s flat therefore represents more than a temporary vacation. It symbolizes an alternative way of living based on openness, affection, and personal freedom. By experiencing that environment, Jaja and Kambili begin to understand that the strict world they grew up in is not the only possible way to live.

inferred_prompt: Write an argumentative essay asking whether the American Dream is still achievable for poor and middle-class Americans. Discuss wealth inequality, unequal opportunity, and the political influence of the wealthy.
text:
The American Dream is often described as the belief that hard work can lead to success, stability, and a better life. However, for many poor and middle-class Americans, that dream has become increasingly difficult to achieve. Growing wealth inequality, unequal access to opportunity, and the political influence of the wealthiest citizens have made upward mobility more difficult.

One major problem is the widening gap between the rich and everyone else. Families with greater wealth can often afford better neighborhoods, stronger schools, tutoring, healthcare, transportation, and professional networks. These advantages can accumulate over time, while low-income families may struggle simply to meet basic expenses.

Unequal opportunity also affects the ability to move upward economically. Children from wealthy families often begin life with resources that lower-income children do not have. Differences in school quality, access to college, technology, and financial support can influence academic and professional outcomes before an individual even enters the workforce.

A third issue is political influence. Wealthy individuals and organizations have more resources to contribute to campaigns, support lobbying efforts, and influence public debate. When economic power can shape public policy, laws may be more likely to protect existing wealth than to expand opportunity for lower-income communities.

Supporters of the traditional American Dream may point out that some people still rise from poverty to wealth through effort and talent. Those examples are important, but individual success stories do not eliminate structural barriers. Hard work matters, but people do not begin from the same starting point.

The American Dream has not disappeared completely, but it is not equally accessible. If the country wants the idea to remain meaningful, it must address the economic and social conditions that prevent many people from having a fair chance to succeed.

His criticism of the government was not rooted in hatred for the United States, but in concern for the direction of the country.

Ultimately, King’s sermon argued that patriotism does not require silence. He believed that speaking honestly about injustice was a form of loyalty.
